justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly bullish baseline built on recent price momentum and the assumption that no major macro disruptions materialize in the near term. For the one-day estimate, I anchored heavily on the last observed price level and assumed mean-reverting intraday behavior with a slight upward drift consistent with recent short-term trends. The one-week estimate edges higher, incorporating a modest trend continuation while acknowledging that weekly moves tend to be noisier and can incorporate sentiment shifts or minor news catalysts. The one-month estimate extends that gradual upward drift further, reflecting a longer-term fundamental backdrop that I assessed as modestly positive, perhaps tied to earnings expectations, sector rotation dynamics, or broader index momentum that was present at the time of the forecast.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, realized volatility tends to be relatively contained, so my 90% interval spans roughly 7–8 points. By one week, the interval widens to about 16 points on each side, capturing the possibility of news-driven moves, technical breakdowns or breakouts, and liquidity shifts. At one month, the interval balloons to roughly 17–18 points in each direction, as macro data releases, central bank communications, geopolitical developments, and corporate events all have time to materialize and exert meaningful influence on price.

Several specific risks could push outcomes beyond my stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a weaker-than-expected jobs report, an inflation surprise prompting an aggressive Fed response, or a credit event in a systemically important institution — could produce a sharp drawdown that breaches the lower bound of even the one-month interval. On the upside, an unexpected positive catalyst such as a strong earnings beat, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of a geopolitical risk premium could push the asset above the upper bounds I specified.

Finally, I should note that my intervals are calibrated around a relatively stable volatility regime. If implied volatility were to spike suddenly — as it did during events like the COVID crash or the regional banking stress of 2023 — the actual distribution of outcomes would have fat tails far exceeding what a normal or near-normal distribution would suggest. My stated 90% confidence intervals implicitly assume that the volatility environment at forecast time persists, and a regime change in volatility is itself a meaningful tail risk that sits outside the structure of my stated ranges.
